chunks: Ali, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Umar Bin Azina, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about the divorce of the coerced and his emancipation (of a slave), so he said: 'His divorce is not a valid divorce, nor is his emancipation a valid emancipation.'
So I said, 'I am a businessman; I pass by the tax collector and with me is wealth.'
So he said: 'Hide it as much as you can, and place it in its proper places.'
So I said, 'And if he makes me swear an oath with the divorce and the emancipation (of a slave)?'
So he said: 'Swear for him.' Then he took a date, and scooped with it from the butter that was in front of him.
So he said: 'I do not mind if you swear for them with the divorce and the emancipation, or I eat it (the date).'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on divorce and freeing a slave if done under coercion by a tax collector?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies that divorce (talaq) and manumission (itq) require specific intent (niyyah) and are not automatically triggered by mere utterance under coercion, a key principle in Shia jurisprudence distinguishing between the spoken word and the legal act. The Imam’s practical advice to hide wealth and his analogy of eating butter with a date illustrate that swearing by these formulas does not invalidate the underlying property or status, emphasizing the flexibility of oaths in daily transactions. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly view that 'coerced' acts lack the voluntary consent necessary for legal validity, protecting individuals from financial exploitation by authorities.

en.hubeali:
Ali, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Umar Bin Azina, from Zurara, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup>, said, ‘I asked him<sup>asws</sup> about a divorce of the coerced, and his emancipation (liberation of a slave).
So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘His divorce is not with a (valid) divorce, nor is his emancipation a (valid) emancipation’.
So I said, ‘I am a businessman. I pass by the tax collector and with me is wealth’.
So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Hide from him according to your capacity, and place it in its (proper) place’.
So I said, ‘And if he makes me swear an oath with the divorce and the emancipation (of a slave)?’

Then he<sup>asws</sup> took a date, so he scooped with it from butter which was in front of him<sup>asws</sup>, so he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘I<sup>asws</sup> don’t mind if you swear for them with the divorce, and the emancipation (of a slave), or I<sup>asws</sup> eat it (the date)’.
en.sarwar: 2. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from ‘Umar ibn ‘Udhaynah from Zurarah who has said the following: “I once asked abu Ja‘far, ‘Alayhi al-Salam,
about the divorce of a man who is coerced and about his setting free slaves. He (the Imam) said, ‘His divorce is not a divorce and his setting free slaves is not valid freedom
/ I then said, ‘I am a merchant and I pass by a one-tenth tax collector, with certain amount of assets with me
/ He (the Imam) said, ‘Keep it concealed as much as you can in their proper place
/ I then asked, ‘What must I do if they ask me to swear about divorce and setting free slaves?’
He (the Imam) said, ‘You can swear for him.’ He (the Imam) then took a piece of date and immersed it in butter in front of him (the Imam).’
He (the Imam) then said, ‘I do not mind about your swearing for divorce and setting free slaves or eating this.’”
